chapter_theme: The wives praise the Lord and hear the king's sermon on desire, harm and release, the Lord is released and cremated by the gods, and Civakan, embracing the maiden Kevala, and the women, who see their bodies as dirt, take up austerity and reach heaven.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who has heard the sage and preaches to his wives
Civakan's wives who sing, hear the sermon and take up austerity
the Lord, the Jina, whose feet are praised and who is released
the gods who honour the Lord's passing
the maiden Kevala, a figure of omniscient knowledge

3098.reading: The women say that the bad deed is a child handed to a nurse named anger, which drinks the breast of desire, grows, and crawls among the painful states of rebirth, and that they have no word of their own beyond the king who told it so.
3098.nuance: Stanza printed in eight half-lines and joined by the edition; the last line's grammar is hard and the speaker is inferred from the 'we' of the next verse.
3098.event: The wives repeat the king's parable of the bad-deed child and its nurse.

claims.claim: a bad deed is like a child nursed by anger and fed on desire that then wanders among painful births

3099.reading: The good deed is a child nursed by the nurse called compassion, who embraces and raises it, and the women say that, freed from the darkness of 'be our king among the gods', they have gone beyond fear.
3099.nuance: The pairing of two nurses, anger and compassion, makes the two kinds of deed two upbringings rather than two amounts; the verse does not say how one becomes the other's nurse.
3099.event: The wives answer the parable with its counterpart of the good-deed child and declare themselves free of fear.

claims.claim: a good deed is a child nursed by compassion that lifts the soul upward

3100.reading: Beyond the light a gem gives and the cool scent a flower gives, the feet are said to give shelter to the dense gnat-swarm of the crowd, and the verse addresses the Lord's red feet that gave this.
3100.nuance: The addressee is not named in the verse; 'the Lord of wealth' is read as the Jina from the surrounding hymn.

claims.claim: the Jina's feet shelter all who come to them, beyond what any pleasure of the senses gives

3101.reading: The Lord's feet, like the sun that rises bearing the day to break the dark at its root, are a spear that cuts the hard-gathered deeds.
3101.nuance: The feet are a weapon rather than a giver of grace: they cut karma as a spear cuts, which differs from a god who forgives it.

claims.claim: worship of the Jina's feet cuts through accumulated karma

3102.reading: The slender women of moon faces and parrot voices are told to sing the Lord's qualities, for the deeds that fell on them have been stopped and do not stay.
3102.event: The women sing the qualities of the Lord and their karma ceases to settle.

claims.claim: singing the Jina's qualities stops karma from settling

3103.reading: As the night-lily opens drinking the moon's rays and drips honey, so those who hail the qualities of the one of perfect knowledge, with no wavering mind, are said to leave their shaking hearts behind.

claims.claim: praise of the omniscient one removes the wavering of the mind

3104.reading: Having worshipped the feet of the Lord of fullness in company with the ascetic heroes, the women ask to worship the light that cuts the dark, and the king gives his answer like a rain of nectar.
3104.event: The wives ask to worship the Lord and the king answers them.

3105.reading: The king says that desire is a bundle of grass that tempts souls into the four states of rebirth, a pen that yields suffering, and that to give up clinging and reach the stainless one's feet is to sell love for the road to the state of release.
3105.nuance: The four states (gods, humans, animals and hell) are not listed in the verse; they are supplied from the Jain scheme the word implies.

claims.claim: clinging draws the soul into the four states of rebirth, and giving it up at the Jina's feet leads to release

3106.reading: The king tells them to worship the golden feet and to hate the strong young men and the full-breasted women who sow desire and reap the disease of birth, since the body so kept is a skin that holds disease.
3106.nuance: The king speaks as a ruler who has just given up many wives; the 'hate the women' language is the sermon's, addressed to women who are about to renounce.

claims.claim: desire for the body is the seed from which the disease of birth grows
the body kept for pleasure is only a bundle of disease and hatred

3107.reading: If a person protects living beings every day as he guards his own life, he will be born lord of sweet lives, an image of joy, a golden soul that rises beyond.
3107.nuance: The reward is rank in a later birth, which makes non-injury a ladder rather than an end; Kural 327 sets the same rule against the loss of one's own life.

claims.claim: one who protects all lives as one's own is reborn in a higher state

3108.reading: If a person makes fire a life for food and does harm, the two deeds kick him down and the fire of the world draws him in, roasts him and sends him into burning flame.
3108.nuance: The first two lines are hard (the nouns turn on a word 'நெருப்புயிர்'); the sense of harm for food is taken from the verbs, so the image of harm by fire is the better-supported reading.

claims.claim: one who harms living beings for his food is cast down by karma into a burning hell

3109.reading: The teaching under the pindi tree is like a rare gem got by one who escaped the great sea of roaring waves, and the good law has taken refuge in a shaded grove of sandal.

claims.claim: the Jina's law is a rare gem to one who has escaped the sea of birth

3110.reading: One who lives in the shade of the wishing-tree will not seek another to give to him, and one who has eaten the nectar under the pindi will not set his mind on the wealth of others.

claims.claim: one who has had the Jina's teaching no longer craves other people's wealth

3111.reading: The king grades souls by metals, from gem and gold through silver and copper to iron, and says he has told this to the end of disease, and urges them to decide, whereupon the women worship and bless him.
3111.nuance: The metal grades are given as a list of ranks; the verse does not say which deeds put a soul at which rank.
3111.event: The king ends the sermon and the women bow and bless him.

claims.claim: souls differ in worth like metals according to the deeds that bind them

3112.reading: Flowers rain from the sky, a full moon seems to pour milk, and honey blossoms seem to walk on the earth as the Lord walks and grants his sight.
3112.event: The Lord walks the earth and the heavens shower flowers on him.

3113.reading: The Lord's teaching, like milk and nectar, sounded in the sky and fed the pure nectar, and flowers were scattered and the directions bowed, and then the day came for him to take the world he had earned.
3113.nuance: 'சாமிநாள்' is read as the day of final release from the line that follows it; the verse itself does not say the word for death.
3113.event: After his last sermon the Lord reaches the day of his passing.

3114.reading: To make those who want gain take their lasting good, the lord set virtue and sat, like the young cool moon, on a seat of his own, and having conquered the four karmas he reached release in festival.
3114.nuance: 'Four karmas' is read as the four that remain after the omniscient one has gone; the verse does not name them. The subject 'kōmān' is the Lord and not Civakan, who comes next.
3114.event: The Lord, having conquered four karmas, reaches release.

claims.claim: conquest of the four binding karmas is what leads to release

3115.reading: Gods gather with drums beating and cloth banners waving, pour a golden rain and flowers, mix sandal and aloe fragrance and crown the Lord.
3115.event: The gods honour the Lord's passing with rain of gold, flowers and perfume.

3116.reading: The flags seem to be swallowed by the red flame, as the rising sun is by the fire, as the bright jewelled body is burnt, and then gods and earth do their auspicious rites, circle the pyre and move away like a shell-loud sea.
3116.nuance: The verse does not say whose body it is; the context of the Lord's release in 3114 supports the Lord.
3116.event: The jewel-bright body of the Lord burns in the flame, and the gods circle it and go away.

3117.reading: The king, whose bright eyes are those of a maiden named Kevala, the knowledge that sees all, embraces her with unblinking eyes, the garland of jasmine on one side and gold on the other, and sinks into a sea of pleasure at the peak of the three worlds.
3117.nuance: The grammar makes the king's identity open: he could be the Lord or Civakan; the book's last ilampakam and 3118 let the reader take Civakan. The maiden is a figure of knowledge and no real woman.
3117.event: The king, now omniscient, embraces the maiden Kevala and sinks in the sea of joy at the top of the three worlds.

claims.claim: omniscience is a bliss at the height of the three worlds, pictured as the embrace of a maiden

3118.reading: Embracing the woman who has no parting, disease, old age, death or birth, he lives in a tall gold mansion where gods carry wine, garlands, sandal, saffron, powder, smoke and lamps.
3118.nuance: The verse mixes heaven's service (wine, garlands) with release; it does not separate the god's heaven from the freed soul's state, and 'இன்றேன்' in line 2 looks corrupt.
3118.event: He lives with the maiden free of ageing and death, served by gods.

claims.claim: the liberated state has no parting, disease, old age, death or birth

3119.reading: The women of spear-bright wide eyes, who walked softly, sat and stood like jasmine crests, with bending waists, reached the great austerity, like one holding up a mountain.
3119.event: The women take up great austerity.

claims.claim: the women's renunciation is a great effort like holding up a mountain

3120.reading: Looking at the bodies they had adorned, as one looks at a green bracelet clinging to a gold doll, the women see the dirt on them and think how to crush the poor birth of woman.
3120.nuance: The poem presents this as the women's own thought, but the narrator's phrase 'ஏழைப் பெண்பிறப்பு' (the poor birth of woman) passes the verdict on women's birth as the work's own.
3120.event: The women see the stain on their own bodies and resolve to end birth as women.

claims.claim: a woman's body is stained and her birth lowly, to be ended by renunciation

3121.reading: Without desire, love or doubt, the women, who did their austerity until the sound of the world ate it, cast off the despised state of woman, became Indras, pure knowledge, and reached heaven.
3121.nuance: Heaven (துறக்கம்) is the end named, not release; the poem's women reach the gods' world, one step below the state the king reached in 3117-3118.
3121.event: The women, having shed their womanhood by austerity, are reborn as Indras and reach heaven.

claims.claim: austerity ends the birth of woman and brings a man's state in heaven

links.note: 3098 gives the bad deed a child nursed by anger and desire; 3099 gives the good deed a child nursed by compassion.
links.teaches: The two verses pair the same upbringing image so that the difference between kinds of deed lies in what feeds them.

links.note: 3101 has the Lord's feet cut through the hard-gathered karma like a blade; Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
links.teaches: The verse gives the means by which the deeds are removed and the Kural gives the assurance that they will not cling.

gains.a: the verse's cutting spear is given an outcome, that the deeds do not attach to the one who praises
gains.b: the Kural's promise that deeds do not cling is given a picture of how, a cutting of the root

links.note: 3101 has worship of the feet cut karma like a weapon; Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped and risen burns the deeds of ages.
links.teaches: Both promise that worship removes karma, but one gives the cutting to an enlightened teacher's feet and the other to a worshipped fire.

gains.a: the Jain feet-as-spear gets a rival agent of the same removal, a burning fire that the Jain verse does not use
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's burning fire gets a rival that cuts by the feet of a liberated one who does not answer prayer

links.note: 3105 pictures desire as grass that lures souls into the four-state pen and says reaching the pure one's feet lets one go to release; Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births.
links.teaches: The verse supplies the trap that the Kural's sea leaves unnamed, and the Kural supplies the crossing the verse only names as going.

gains.a: the verse's pen of four states gets the picture of a sea crossed, which turns the escape into a swim
gains.b: the Kural's sea of births gets a reason people are in it, the grass of desire, and a price for crossing, love sold

links.note: 3107 says that guarding all lives as one's own brings a high birth; Kural 327 says not to kill even if one's own life is the price.
links.teaches: The verse makes non-injury pay in a later birth, and the Kural cuts the rule loose from payment even at the price of one's life.

gains.a: the verse's reward for protection is tested by the case where protection costs the protector his life
gains.b: the Kural's absolute rule gets the Jain account of what the careful guarder wins in later births

links.note: 3108 has the one who harms for food thrown by two deeds into burning flame; Kural 320 says pains rest on those who caused pain.
links.teaches: The verse names the form the returning pain takes, a hell of fire, which the Kural's general law does not.

gains.a: the verse's hell is shown as one case of a general law that pain returns to its cause
gains.b: the Kural's law gets a specific place and fire where the pain lands

links.note: 3117 pictures omniscience as a maiden embraced by the king at the top of the worlds, the self still distinct; Tirumanthiram 134 says those who feel the teacher's word become the reality, like ghee mixed in milk.
links.teaches: Both end in bliss, but the Cintamani keeps lover and beloved two, while the Tirumanthiram dissolves the self into what it meets.

gains.a: the verse's embrace is shown as release that keeps a separate self, which the milk-and-ghee image of union would remove
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's merging gets a rival picture where the freed one stays apart and enjoys

links.note: 3118 has the king live with a woman who has no old age or death; Naladiyar 14 has the once-desired woman bent over a staff and a torment.
links.teaches: One text shows what the loved woman will become, and the other the woman who never becomes it.

gains.a: the verse's ageless bride is shown as the answer to the old woman the quatrain describes
gains.b: the Naladiyar's bent old woman gets the Jain promise of a partner who does not age, offered to those who give up the first kind

links.note: 3120 has the women see the dirt on their adorned bodies and think of ending woman-birth; Naladiyar 46 breaks the woman into entrails, fat, blood and bone and asks which part she is.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives the analysis of the body's parts and the verse shows women applying a like seeing to themselves.

gains.a: the verse's women get the reasoned list of parts that grounds their disgust, so their turn is more than a mood
gains.b: the Naladiyar's list, offered to men about women, gets a case where women use it on their own bodies

links.note: 3106 tells the women to hate the body kept for desire; 3120 shows them doing it, seeing their adorned bodies as stained.
links.teaches: The sermon's advice to hate the body and the women's act of seeing it as dirt are the same turn, the teaching and then its keeping.

links.note: 3116 has the pyre burn the Lord's jewel-bright body with gods circling and rejoicing; Naladiyar 24 has the drums beat three times and the corpse be covered and the fire taken up.
links.teaches: The same flame ends an ordinary corpse in grief and a Lord's body in festival, so the pyre's meaning depends on who is burning.

gains.a: the festival pyre is shown in contrast with the common corpse's plain burning, which the gods' honours dress up
gains.b: the quatrain's grieved burning gets a body whose burning is celebrated because nothing of the person is lost

links.note: 3105 says that giving up clinging at the pure one's feet lets one reach the state of release; 3121 shows the women, free of desire and love, reaching heaven.
links.teaches: The promise to the women's sermon is kept, though what they reach is heaven rather than the release the verse named.

links.note: 3121 sends the women who gave up desire to heaven as Indras; Kural 346 says one who cuts off 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'.
links.teaches: The verse ends in the gods' world and the Kural says release lies above it, so the same renunciation is given two different ends.

gains.a: the verse's heaven is shown as a stop below where the Kural puts the one who has left 'I' and 'mine'
gains.b: the Kural's world above the gods gets a case of renouncers who stop at the gods' world

source_issues: Many stanzas are printed in eight half-lines and were joined into four lines by the edition.
3117 and 3118 leave the king's identity open between the Lord and Civakan.
